questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a push factor?
options: A condition in the domestic market that drives a business to seek opportunities abroad
An attraction of a foreign market that draws a business towards it
A government incentive to export
A tariff imposed by a foreign government
questions.why: Saturation and competition at home are the two push factors named in the specification.
whyNot: That is a pull factor.
An incentive would be a pull factor.
A tariff is a barrier, not a push factor.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines off-shoring?
options: Relocating a business's own activity to another country while keeping it within the business
Contracting an activity out to another business
Selling products in another country
Registering a company in a low-tax country
questions.why: Off-shoring is about location; outsourcing is about who performs the activity.
whyNot: That is outsourcing.
That is exporting.
That is a tax arrangement, not off-shoring of activity.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines outsourcing?
options: Contracting an activity out to another business, whether at home or abroad
Moving the business's own activity to another country
Buying raw materials from a foreign supplier
Selling a division of the business
questions.why: Control is reduced because the activity is performed by a supplier rather than by the business itself.
whyNot: That is off-shoring.
Buying inputs is ordinary purchasing, not outsourcing an activity.
That is a divestment.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a saturated market?
options: A market in which almost all potential customers already own the product
A market with very high prices
A market with only one supplier
A market growing faster than the economy
questions.why: Growth is then limited to replacement demand, which is why it is a push factor.
whyNot: High prices do not indicate saturation.
That is a monopoly.
A fast-growing market is the opposite of saturated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pull factor named in the specification?
options: Risk spreading and economies of scale
Saturated domestic markets
Intense domestic competition
High domestic regulation
questions.why: Increased sales and profitability, risk spreading and economies of scale are the named pull factors.
whyNot: That is a push factor.
That is a push factor.
That is a push factor.

questions.stem: What is the limit of risk spreading through operating in many countries?
options: Economies are increasingly correlated, so a global downturn hits everywhere at once
Risk cannot be spread at all
Operating in many countries increases the risk in each one
Risk spreading only works for service businesses
questions.why: A business with a hundred markets still has one global exposure, which is why risk spreading is not complete protection.
whyNot: It genuinely reduces country-specific risk.
Diversification does not raise the risk in each individual market.
It applies to any business.

questions.stem: Which pull factor is strongest for a business with very high fixed costs?
options: Economies of scale, because higher volume spreads the fixed costs
Risk spreading, because fixed costs vary by country
Extending the product life cycle
Government incentives
questions.why: Research, development and brand-building costs are spread over a much larger volume, so unit cost falls with every extra unit.
whyNot: Fixed costs are spread by volume rather than by geography.
Life-cycle extension is a separate benefit.
Incentives are usually a smaller consideration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a risk of outsourcing rather than off-shoring?
options: Loss of control over quality and the risk of supplier power
Cultural and time-zone difficulties in managing your own staff
Higher wage costs in the home country
The need to build a new factory abroad
questions.why: Outsourcing hands the activity to a supplier, so quality, reliability and loss of in-house expertise are the risks.
whyNot: That is a risk of off-shoring your own operation.
Outsourcing usually reduces wage costs rather than raising them.
Building a factory would be off-shoring, not outsourcing.

questions.stem: Why are off-shoring decisions often regretted?
options: The saving is measurable and immediate while the costs are largely non-financial and delayed
The saving never materialises at all
Off-shoring is usually unlawful
The costs are always larger than the savings
questions.why: Naming that asymmetry is worth a mark, because it explains why the decision looks better on a spreadsheet than in practice.
whyNot: Cost savings are usually real in the short term.
Off-shoring is lawful and common.
Sometimes the savings dominate; the point is the timing and measurability.

questions.stem: Why does it matter whether a business is pushed or pulled abroad?
options: A pushed business is under pressure and may accept a weaker opportunity than it should
Pushed businesses are always more successful abroad
Pull factors are never genuine
Push and pull factors never occur together
questions.why: A business pulled by a genuinely attractive market is choosing from strength and can walk away, which changes the recommendation.
whyNot: Pressure tends to worsen decision quality, not improve it.
Pull factors are frequently the dominant reason.
They almost always operate together.

questions.stem: Why can selling a mature product in a growing market extend its life cycle profitably?
options: Development costs are sunk and production is already at scale
Mature products cost more to make
Growing markets always pay higher prices
Life cycles are not affected by the market entered
questions.why: The marketing also does not have to educate the market about the product category, which lowers the launch cost.
whyNot: Mature products are usually cheaper to produce.
Price depends on the market's income and competition.
Entering a market at a different stage changes the cycle directly.

options: Contracting manufacture to a firm in another country, carrying both sets of risks
Moving your own factory abroad and keeping it in-house
Outsourcing to a domestic supplier only
Exporting through a foreign agent
questions.why: It is the most common arrangement and combines the loss of control of outsourcing with the distance of off-shoring.
whyNot: That is off-shoring alone.
That is domestic outsourcing.
Using an agent is a distribution arrangement.

questions.stem: Which indicator most clearly signals a saturated domestic market?
options: High market penetration combined with low market growth
High market growth with low penetration
A rising number of new entrants
A falling exchange rate
questions.why: That combination describes a mature or declining market, so growth must come from elsewhere.
whyNot: That describes a growing market.
New entrants suggest the market is still attractive.
The exchange rate says nothing about saturation.

questions.stem: Why is expansion abroad driven almost entirely by push factors for a business in a very small economy?
options: A tiny dispersed home market caps volume whatever its market share
Small economies never have attractive foreign markets nearby
Small economies prohibit domestic growth
Pull factors only apply to large businesses
questions.why: The option of growing at home simply is not available, which makes the push-pull distinction concrete.
whyNot: Nearby markets may be very attractive; that is a separate matter.
No such prohibition exists.
Pull factors apply to businesses of any size.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an argument for outsourcing?
options: Access to specialist capability with lower fixed costs and greater flexibility
Complete control over quality and timing
Retention of all in-house expertise
Shorter and simpler supply chains
questions.why: It also lets management concentrate attention on the business's core activities.
whyNot: Control is reduced, which is the main drawback.
In-house expertise tends to be lost.
Supply chains usually become longer and more complex.

questions.stem: Which alternative to off-shoring should an evaluation usually consider?
options: Automation at home, or outsourcing without relocating
Increasing the selling price to cover the higher domestic cost
Closing the business entirely
Waiting until wages fall domestically
questions.why: Considering the alternatives is part of a full evaluation, and automation addresses the cost problem without the control and reputational risks.
whyNot: A price rise may simply lose volume to competitors who have off-shored.
Closure is not a realistic alternative to a cost decision.
Domestic wages rarely fall.
